fields.foundation: The Ghana Empire, known internally as Wagadou, is often linked to the Tichitt stone-settlement culture of Mauritania, traceable archaeologically to the second millennium BCE at Dhar Tichitt and Dhar Walata. The Soninke people who built it were iron-working and militarily capable. They occupied the zone between the goldfields of Bambuk and Bure to the south and the Saharan caravan routes leading north to Berber and eventually Arab markets. The spread of the camel across the western Sahara in the early centuries CE turned irregular desert crossings into a regular trade network, and Wagadou was already placed to dominate it. The astronomer al-Fazari, writing in the late eighth century, referred to Ghana as the land of gold, the earliest known reference to the kingdom in Arabic sources. Soninke oral tradition credits the formal unification of the clans to Dinga Cissé, and many historians place the emergence of the empire as a recognisable state by around 750 CE. The title ghana, often interpreted as war chief, was applied by Arab geographers to the king and eventually named the empire. Ghana rose for economic rather than military reasons: it stood between two things other people wanted to exchange.
fields.socioeconomy: The Ghana Empire drew its wealth from taxing trade. The king imposed duties on goods entering and leaving the realm, taxing salt moving south from Saharan mines and gold moving north from the southern fields at the same time. All gold nuggets found within the kingdom were reserved for the king, while subjects could trade gold dust freely, a deliberate mechanism that controlled supply and prevented the price from collapsing. Al-Bakri's celebrated description of the court, completed in 1068, recorded horses caparisoned in gold-embroidered cloth, pages bearing gold-mounted shields and swords, and even guard dogs wearing collars of gold and silver. Ibn Hawqal, writing around 977, declared Ghana's king the wealthiest monarch on earth because of his gold. The capital, generally identified with Koumbi Saleh, was a double city: the royal town of El-Ghaba with its palace and sacred grove, and a separate Muslim merchants' town six miles distant with twelve mosques and surrounding gardens. The two towns show a society that had taken in Islamic commercial networks without converting its political elite. The king kept his traditional legitimacy and accommodated the faith of his most valuable trading partners.
fields.military: Ghana's military power was substantial, but it was not the main instrument of its dominance. Al-Bakri recorded that the king could field 200,000 warriors, of whom more than 40,000 were archers. The figures are almost certainly inflated, but they indicate a large capacity to mobilise compared with regional rivals. Iron weaponry and cavalry gave Soninke forces a significant advantage over many neighbouring peoples. The empire's most significant offensive achievement was the capture, traditionally dated to around 992, of Awdaghast, the oasis town at the southern end of the western trans-Saharan route, previously dominated by Sanhaja Berbers. This conquest gave Ghana direct control over the main desert terminus of the gold-salt trade and was the furthest extent of the empire's expansion. Otherwise military power was used mainly to enforce tributary relationships with subordinate kingdoms across the western Sudan, extracting regular payments that supplemented trade revenues. Ghana never attempted to conquer the goldfields themselves, whether from deliberate restraint or because of geography.
fields.governance: The Ghana Empire was a hereditary monarchy that ruled through tributaries. The geographer al-Yaqubi, writing in the late ninth century, noted that the king of Ghana had other kings under his authority, which confirms a layered hierarchy of vassal relationships rather than direct territorial administration. Succession was matrilineal, passing to the king's sister's son, a custom al-Bakri documented explicitly. The royal court maintained ministers and provincial governors responsible for administering outlying territories and enforcing trade regulations, and al-Bakri noted that the king's interpreters, treasurer, and most ministers were drawn from the Muslim community. The king dispensed justice personally in public audience, surrounded by elaborate ceremony. In the capital's two towns, Muslim merchants lived under their own law in their own quarter, while royal religious traditions were maintained separately. The empire could thus use Islamic commercial institutions without subjecting its political legitimacy to Islamic legal authority. The arrangement held for centuries until the Almoravid era, when the ruling house appears to have adopted Islam in the late eleventh century.
fields.impact: Ghana's command of the western trans-Saharan trade made it the channel through which West Africa entered the medieval world economy. Gold going north through Wagadou supplied the mints of North Africa and Muslim Spain and, through them, the wider Mediterranean, so that Ghana's fiscal control indirectly affected monetary systems across three continents. Its successor states inherited and adapted the empire's tributary structure, twin-town urban design, and gold taxation mechanism. The Mali Empire, which absorbed Wagadou in the thirteenth century, repeated and expanded Ghana's trans-Saharan commercial system. When the Gold Coast gained independence in 1957, Kwame Nkrumah chose this empire's name to assert a pre-colonial African tradition of statehood and sophistication, seven centuries after the original kingdom had ceased to exist.
fields.decline: Ghana's collapse was not sudden. The Almoravid capture of Awdaghast in 1054 reversed some sixty years of Ghanaian control over the northern trade terminus, and the Sack of Koumbi Saleh by the Almoravids, traditionally dated to 1076, reduced the empire for a time to a tributary of the Almoravid movement. After the death of the Almoravid leader Abu Bakr ibn Umar in 1087 the Soninke recovered their independence, but trade routes were already shifting eastward towards the Niger bend, and Ghana no longer held the position that had made it supreme. Prolonged Sahel drought in the twelfth century damaged agricultural production. The Sosso kingdom of Kaniaga, a former vassal, rose to dominance under Sumanguru Kante and took over Wagadou in the early thirteenth century. After Sundiata Keita defeated Sumanguru at Kirina around 1235, the remnant of Ghana was incorporated into the Mali Empire, its capital traditionally said to have been abandoned around 1240.
fields.summary: For centuries Wagadou dominated one of the medieval world's most lucrative trade corridors without owning a single goldfield. The Ghana Empire's power rested on taxing what it could not possess, not on territorial control.
fields.teaser: Often regarded as the first great empire of West Africa, Ghana controlled the trans-Saharan gold and salt trade, becoming fabulously wealthy long before European contact with the region.
fields.t0: Wagadou, the Soninke kingdom Arab writers called Ghana, sat between West Africa's goldfields and the Saharan caravan routes.
fields.t1: It grew rich by taxing gold going north and salt going south, and its gold supplied mints across North Africa and Muslim Spain.
fields.t2: Almoravid attacks, shifting trade routes and drought broke its power; Mali absorbed what remained in the thirteenth century.
fields.dyk: Ghana's king kept every gold nugget found in the kingdom for himself, letting subjects trade only gold dust, a deliberate way to stop the price of gold from collapsing.
